item.text: {"text":"Padding correctness comes first. PyTorch GRU equations contain recurrent transformations and biases, so zero input embeddings do not guarantee unchanged hidden states. Explicitly preserve state on padding: `h = where(item_id != 0, GRUCell(x, h), h_previous)` at every recurrent layer. Read the greatest nonpadding index; `count-1` is incorrect for left padding. In evaluation mode, compare identical histories with different amounts of leading padding, checking final features, candidate scores, and training/predictor agreement. These checks follow from the [GRU equations](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html). [Repeated Padding (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06372) reports substantial GRU4Rec improvements, but deliberately repeats interactions as augmentation; it does not establish padding invariance.\n\nRelated research supports adaptive retention without establishing this exact proposal: [PRIDES (2025)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10976648) studies interests disappearing and reappearing within sessions; [heterogeneous interest-duration modeling (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11127) models interest changes through hidden semi-Markov states. An earlier [hierarchical recurrent model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12674) explicitly introduces interest-drift gates. Practical hypothesis: after correctness checks pass, condition one jointly trained GRU’s retention gate on the observed item embedding, previous state, and their mismatch; optionally examine observed timestamp gaps. Treat this as soft adaptive forgetting, not a verified change-point detector. Compare against the corrected GRU using fixed macro validation HR@10, retaining one checkpoint per category. No reviewed source establishes gains for this exact gate on the pinned four-category benchmark; temporal benefits remain unmeasured."}
